lines.text: Even if you've never held a controller, Link feels familiar.
A kid leaves home, faces impossible problems, and keeps going.
It's one of the oldest stories we have.

sections.title: The hero with a thousand faces

lines.text: In 1949, the mythologist Joseph Campbell published The Hero with a Thousand Faces.
Reading myths from all over the world, he kept meeting the same figure: one hero, wearing different faces.
Leave home. Face trials. Return changed.
Carl Jung called recurring figures like this archetypes.
Campbell's real discovery wasn't a formula. It was the recurrence itself.
So why does every culture keep inventing the same hero? Hold that thought.
Take Link in Ocarina of Time, from 1998: an ordinary boy from the forest, until the Great Deku Tree calls him to adventure.
He draws the Master Sword, and wakes seven years later in a Hyrule fallen to darkness.
Like every player, he fails, and tries again.
And across the series, the hero keeps returning in new forms.
Nearly four thousand years ago, Gilgamesh tried to defeat death.
His solution failed, and he came home changed.
Heracles faced his labours. When two didn't count, he did two more.
Odysseus spent ten years getting home.
And in Arthurian legend, only the true king could draw the sword from the stone.
Sound familiar?
The faces keep changing.
Frodo carries the burden. Sam carries Frodo. And Aragorn returns as king.
Master Chief finishes the fight.
Luke answers the call.
Major Kusanagi asks what makes her herself.
Guts struggles against fate.
Goku trains past every limit.
Naruto never goes back on his word.
Nausicaä studies the poisoned forest, and finds the real problem is the soil.
Neo chooses.
And K learns he isn't the chosen one, and does the heroic thing anyway. He brings Deckard home to his daughter.
No hero solves problems alone.
The mentor passes on knowledge: Merlin, Gandalf, Krishna, the Great Deku Tree.
The shadow is the problem given a face: Ganondorf, Vader, Ravana.
The trickster breaks the rules and exposes mistakes: Loki, Anansi, Sun Wukong.
And the wise guide lights the way: Princess Zelda, or Guanyin.

sections.title: Why the hero keeps coming back

lines.text: So why does the same hero keep appearing?
Campbell found the pattern. Karl Popper and David Deutsch help explain it.
Popper argued that all life is problem solving. We guess, we make mistakes, and we correct them.
Deutsch went further. Every person, he argues, is a universal explainer: able, in principle, to understand anything that can be understood.
He put it in two lines. Problems are inevitable. Problems are soluble.
A world full of problem-solvers keeps telling stories about one.
That's why the thousand faces feel like one.
The hero is what greatness looks like against a problem: wrong sometimes, tested always, and never out of hope.
Your next problem is already waiting. Go meet it.
And subscribe for more.
